{{Short description|Equation in physics}}
{{electromagnetism}}

In [[electromagnetism]] and applications, an '''inhomogeneous electromagnetic wave equation''', or '''nonhomogeneous electromagnetic wave equation''', is one of a set of [[wave equation|wave equations]] describing the propagation of [[electromagnetic waves]] generated by nonzero source [[electric charge|charges]] and [[electric current|currents]]. The source terms in the wave equations make the [[partial differential equations]] [[Homogeneous differential equation#Homogeneous linear differential equations|inhomogeneous]], if the source terms are zero the equations reduce to the [[Homogeneous differential equation|homogeneous]] [[electromagnetic wave equation|electromagnetic wave equations]], which follow from [[Maxwell's equations]].

== Maxwell's equations ==
<!---These are here to save the reader having to go back and forth to the Maxwell's equations article--->

For reference, [[Maxwell's equations]] are summarized below in [[SI units]] and [[Gaussian units]]. They govern the [[electric field]] '''E''' and [[magnetic field]] '''B''' due to a source [[charge density]] ''ρ'' and [[current density]] '''J''':

{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center; padding-left: 1.5em;"
|-
! scope="col" style="width: 15em;" | Name
! scope="col" | SI units
! scope="col" | Gaussian units
|-
! scope="row" | [[Gauss's law]]
| <math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} = \frac {\rho} {\varepsilon_0}</math>
|<math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} = 4\pi\rho </math>
|-
! scope="row" | [[Gauss's law for magnetism]]
| <math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0</math>
| <math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0</math>
|-
! scope="row" | Maxwell–Faraday equation ([[Faraday's law of induction]])
|<math>\nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}} {\partial t}</math>
| <math>\nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{1}{c} \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}} {\partial t}</math>
|-
! scope="row" | [[Ampère's circuital law]] (with Maxwell's addition)
| <math>\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0\left(\mathbf{J} + \varepsilon_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}} {\partial t} \right) </math>
|<math>\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{c} \left(4\pi\mathbf{J} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} \right)</math>
|-
|}

where ''ε''<sub>0</sub> is the [[vacuum permittivity]] and ''μ''<sub>0</sub> is the [[vacuum permeability]]. Throughout, the relation
<math display="block">\varepsilon_0 \mu_0 = \dfrac{1}{c^2}</math>
is also used.

==SI units==

=== E and B fields ===

[[Maxwell's equations]] can directly give inhomogeneous wave equations for the electric field '''E''' and magnetic field '''B'''.<ref>{{harvnb|Jackson|1998|p=246}}</ref> Substituting [[Gauss's law|Gauss's law for electricity]] and [[Ampère's circuital law#Extending the original law: the Ampère–Maxwell equation |Ampère's law]] into the [[curl (mathematics)|curl]] of [[Faraday's law of induction]], and using the [[Vector calculus identities#Curl of curl|curl of the curl identity]] {{nowrap|1=∇ × (∇ × '''X''') = ∇(∇ ⋅ '''X''') − ∇<sup>2</sup>'''X'''}} (The last term in the right side is the [[vector Laplacian]], not Laplacian applied on scalar functions.) gives the wave equation for the [[electric field]] '''E''':
<math display="block">\dfrac{1}{c^2}\dfrac{\partial^2\mathbf{ E}}{\partial t^2}-\nabla^2\mathbf{ E} = -\left(\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_0} \nabla\rho+\mu_0\dfrac{\partial\mathbf{ J}}{\partial t}\right)\,.</math>

Similarly substituting [[Gauss's law for magnetism]] into the curl of [[Ampère's circuital law]] (with Maxwell's additional time-dependent term), and using the curl of the curl identity, gives the wave equation for the [[magnetic field]] '''B''':
<math display="block">\dfrac{1}{c^2}\dfrac{\partial^2 \mathbf{B}}{\partial t^2}-\nabla^2\mathbf{ B} = \mu_0 \nabla\times\mathbf{J}\,.</math>

The left hand sides of each equation correspond to wave motion (the [[D'Alembert operator]] acting on the fields), while the right hand sides are the wave sources. The equations imply that EM waves are generated if there are gradients in charge density ''ρ'', circulations in current density '''J''', time-varying current density, or any mixture of these.

The above equation for the electric field can be transformed to a homogeneous wave equation with a so called damping term if we study a problem where Ohm's law in differential form <math dislpay="block"> \mathbf{J_f}=\sigma\mathbf{E}</math> holds (we assume <math dislpay="block"> \mathbf{J_b}=0</math> that is we are dealing with homogeneous conductors that have relative permeability and permittivity around 1), and by substituting <math display="block"> \dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\nabla\rho=\nabla(\nabla \cdot\mathbf{E})</math> from the differential form of Gauss's law and 
<math dislpay="block"> \mathbf{J=J_b+J_f}=\sigma\mathbf{E}</math>. 

The final homogeneous equation with only the unknown electric field and its partial derivatives is 
<math display="block">\dfrac{1}{c^2}\dfrac{\partial^2\mathbf{ E}}{\partial t^2}-\nabla^2\mathbf{ E} +\nabla(\nabla  \cdot \mathbf{E})+\sigma\mu_0\dfrac{\partial\mathbf{ E}}{\partial t}=0.</math>
The solutions for the above homogeneous equation for the electric field are infinitely many and we must specify boundary conditions for the electric field in order to find specific solutions. 

These forms of the wave equations are not often used in practice, as the source terms are inconveniently complicated. A simpler formulation more commonly encountered in the literature and used in theory use the [[electromagnetic potential]] formulation, presented next.

=== A and ''φ'' potential fields ===

Introducing the [[electric potential]] ''φ'' (a [[scalar potential]]) and the [[Magnetic vector potential|magnetic potential]] '''A''' (a [[vector potential]]) defined from the '''E''' and '''B''' fields by:
<math display="block"> \mathbf{E} = - \nabla \varphi - \frac{\partial \mathbf{A}}{\partial t} \,,\quad \mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A} \,.</math>

The four Maxwell's equations in a vacuum with charge ''ρ'' and current '''J''' sources reduce to two equations, Gauss's law for electricity is:
<math display="block"> \nabla^2 \varphi + \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left ( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{A} \right ) = - \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0} \rho \,, </math>
where <math> \nabla^2 </math> here is the [[Laplace operator|Laplacian]] applied on scalar functions, and the Ampère-Maxwell law is:
<math display="block"> \nabla^2 \mathbf{A} - \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{A}}{\partial t^2} - \nabla \left ( \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{A} \right ) = - \mu_0 \mathbf{J} \, </math>
where <math> \nabla^2 </math> here is the [[vector Laplacian]] applied on vector fields. The source terms are now much simpler, but the wave terms are less obvious. Since the potentials are not unique, but have [[Gauge theory#Classical gauge theory|gauge]] freedom, these equations can be simplified by [[gauge fixing]]. A common choice is the [[Lorenz gauge condition]]:
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{A} = 0 </math>

Then the nonhomogeneous wave equations become uncoupled and symmetric in the potentials:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 \nabla^2 \varphi - \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2 \varphi}{\partial t^2} &= - \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\rho \,, \\[2.75ex]
 \nabla^2 \mathbf{A} - \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{A}}{\partial t^2} &= - \mu_0 \mathbf{J} \,.
\end{align}</math>

For reference, in [[cgs units]] these equations are
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
 \nabla^2 \varphi - \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2 \varphi}{\partial t^2} &= - 4 \pi \rho \\[2ex]
 \nabla^2 \mathbf{A} - \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{A}}{\partial t^2} &= - \frac{4 \pi}{c} \mathbf{J}
\end{align} </math>
with the Lorenz gauge condition
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{c} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{A} = 0\,.</math>

==Covariant form of the inhomogeneous wave equation==

{{see also|Covariant formulation of classical electromagnetism}}

[[Image:Time dilation02.gif|right|frame|Time dilation in transversal motion. The requirement that the speed of light is constant in every inertial reference frame leads to the [[Special relativity|theory of relativity]] ]]
The [[Formulation of Maxwell's equations in special relativity|relativistic Maxwell's equations]] can be written in [[Covariance and contravariance of vectors|covariant]] form as
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\Box A^{\mu} &\ \stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{def}}{=}\ \partial_{\beta} \partial^{\beta} A^{\mu} \ \stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{def}}{=}\ {A^{\mu , \beta}}_{\beta} = - \mu_0 J^{\mu} && \text{SI} \\[1.15ex]
\Box A^{\mu} &\ \stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{def}}{=}\ \partial_{\beta} \partial^{\beta} A^{\mu} \ \stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{def}}{=}\ {A^{\mu , \beta}}_{\beta} = - \tfrac{4 \pi}{c} J^{\mu} && \text{cgs}
\end{align} </math>
where
<math display="block">\Box = \partial_{\beta} \partial^{\beta} = \nabla^2 - \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{ \partial^2} { \partial t^2}</math>
is the [[d'Alembert operator]],
<math display="block">J^{\mu} = \left(c \rho, \mathbf{J} \right)</math>
is the [[four-current]],
<math display="block"> \frac{\partial}{\partial x^a} \ \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ \partial_a \ \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ {}_{,a} \ \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ (\partial/\partial ct, \nabla)</math>
is the [[Four-gradient|4-gradient]], and
<math display="block">\begin{align}
A^{\mu} &= (\varphi/c, \mathbf{A}) && \text{SI} \\[1ex]
A^{\mu} &= (\varphi, \mathbf{A} ) && \text{cgs}
\end{align} </math>
is the [[electromagnetic four-potential]] with the [[Lorenz gauge]] condition
<math display="block">\partial_{\mu} A^{\mu} = 0\,.</math>

==Curved spacetime==

The electromagnetic wave equation is modified in two ways in [[curved spacetime]], the derivative is replaced with the [[covariant derivative]] and a new term that depends on the curvature appears (SI units).
<math display="block"> - {A^{\alpha ; \beta}}_{ \beta} + {R^{\alpha}}_{\beta} A^{\beta} = \mu_0 J^{\alpha} </math>
where
<math display="block"> {R^\alpha}_{\beta} </math>
is the [[Ricci curvature tensor]]. Here the semicolon indicates covariant differentiation. To obtain the equation in cgs units, replace the permeability with 4''π''/''c''.

The [[Lorenz gauge condition]] in curved spacetime is assumed:
<math display="block"> {A^{\mu}}_{ ; \mu} = 0 \,. </math>

The wave equation for the [[electromagnetic tensor]] <math> F_{\mu \nu}  </math> has the form:<ref>{{cite journal |last=Fedosin|first=S. G.| title= Analysis of solution of equations for magnetic field of rotating ball using polynomials |url=https://rdcu.be/fgOlw |journal= Discover Physics |volume=2|article-number=5| date=2026-05-04| doi=10.1007/s44418-026-00008-w|s2cid=287968904 }}</ref>

:<math> \nabla^\sigma \nabla_\sigma F_{\mu \nu} = \mu_0 \nabla_\mu J_\nu -\mu_0 \nabla_\nu J_\mu - F_{\nu \rho} R^\rho {}_\mu + F_{\mu \rho} R^\rho {}_\nu +R_{\mu \nu \lambda \eta} F^{\eta \lambda}.  </math>

== Solutions to the inhomogeneous electromagnetic wave equation ==
[[Image:Electromagnetic wave equation.png|thumb|500px|right|Retarded spherical wave. The source of the wave occurs at time {{math|''t''{{'}}}}. The wavefront moves away from the source as time increases for {{nowrap|''t'' > ''t''{{'}}}}. For advanced solutions, the wavefront moves backwards in time from the source {{nowrap|''t'' < ''t''{{'}}}}.]]

In the case that there are no boundaries surrounding the sources, the solutions (cgs units) of the nonhomogeneous wave equations are
<math display="block"> \varphi (\mathbf{r}, t) = \int \frac{ \delta \left ( t' + \frac{1}{c} { \left | \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}' \right | } - t \right ) } {\left | \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}' \right |} \rho (\mathbf{r}', t') \, d^3\mathbf{r}' dt' </math>
and
<math display="block"> \mathbf{A} (\mathbf{r}, t) = \int \frac{ \delta \left ( t' + \frac{1}{c}{ \left | \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}' \right | } - t \right ) } { \left | \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}' \right | } \frac{\mathbf{J} (\mathbf{r}', t')}{c} \, d^3\mathbf{r}' dt' </math>
where
<math display="block"> \delta \left ( t' + \tfrac{1}{c} { \left | \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}' \right | } - t \right ) </math>
is a [[Dirac delta function]].

These solutions are known as the retarded [[Lorenz gauge]] potentials. They represent a [[Superposition principle|superposition]] of spherical light waves traveling outward from the sources of the waves, from the present into the future.

There are also advanced solutions (cgs units)
<math display="block"> \varphi (\mathbf{r}, t) = \int \frac { \delta \left ( t' - \tfrac{1}{c} { \left | \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}' \right | } - t \right ) } { \left | \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}' \right | } \rho (\mathbf{r}', t') \, d^3\mathbf{r}' dt' </math>
and
<math display="block"> \mathbf{A} (\mathbf{r}, t) = \int \frac{ \delta \left ( t' - \tfrac{1}{c}{ \left | \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}' \right | } - t \right ) } { \left | \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}' \right | } { \mathbf{J} (\mathbf{r}', t') \over c } \, d^3\mathbf{r}' dt' \,.</math>

These represent a superposition of spherical waves travelling from the future into the present.
